title: Sorting
summary: Put data in order so that comparisons, merging, and searching become simple and fast.
keyPoints: Comparison sorting cannot beat O(n log n) in the general case.
Merge sort splits, sorts, and merges; it is stable and predictable at O(n log n).
Quick sort partitions around a pivot; it is fast in practice but has an O(n²) worst case.
Counting sort avoids comparisons when values come from a small integer range.
A custom comparator is often the whole solution to an interval or scheduling problem.

complexity.note: O(n²) worst case with bad pivots; call-stack space is O(log n) average and O(n) worst case.
Fast for tiny or nearly sorted inputs.

commonMistakes: Assuming the language's sort is stable when the problem depends on original order.
Writing a comparator that can return inconsistent results, such as subtracting large numbers that overflow.
Re-sorting inside a loop instead of sorting once before the loop.
Using comparison sort when a counting approach would be linear for a small fixed range.
interviewNotes: If sorting is acceptable, say that it changes the input order, then state the new complexity.
For interval problems, sort by start or by end; the right choice depends on whether you are merging or scheduling.
For top-k problems, ask whether a heap can avoid sorting everything.

checkYourself.question: Why is merge sort a good fit for linked lists?
checkYourself.answer: Merging two sorted lists only needs pointer changes and no random access, so the merge step is O(1) extra space per merge.

checkYourself.question: When is counting sort a better choice than comparison sort?
checkYourself.answer: When values are integers in a small, known range, so a counter array is cheap and the O(n + k) pass beats O(n log n).

checkYourself.question: Why sort by end time for the classic maximum-meetings problem?
checkYourself.answer: Choosing the meeting that ends earliest leaves the most room for later meetings. Sorting by start does not give that guarantee.
